**In the wet, rain-slicked dark of the alley, hunger ruled.**

It gnawed at him like a living thing, older than the brick walls that hemmed them in, deeper than the drip of water from broken gutters. The vampire’s mouth flooded with need—sharp, copper-edged, insistent. Every distant heartbeat in the city felt like a taunt, but the one close by… that was a drumbeat against his ribs. The victim had turned the wrong corner, footsteps too light, breath too quick. Foolish. Alive.

He moved without sound. One moment empty space and the stink of refuse; the next, two shadows pressed into the deepest recess behind a dumpster. A gloved hand clamped over the mouth before the scream could form. Eyes went wide—shock, then the beginning of terror as cold breath ghosted across the throat.

“Shhh,” the vampire murmured, almost gentle. The hunger made the words vibrate. “It will end.”

He tilted the head aside. The carotid pulsed under thin skin, a frantic invitation. Fang-tips pressed, parted flesh with surgical precision. Twin puncture wounds bloomed—small, clean, almost elegant—then dark blood welled instantly, hot and shockingly alive. The first swallow hit like fire through dry wood. Infinitely better than any bottle, any pale imitation. The hunger roared in triumph and demanded more.

He drank.

Rhythm became everything: the suck, the slow thaw of strength returning to his limbs, the thrum of borrowed life flooding starved veins. The victim’s body jerked once, then went slack against him. Muffled sounds turned to wet gasps. Hands that had scrabbled at his coat weakened, fingers uncurling. Knees buckled. He held the weight easily, almost tenderly, refusing to waste a drop.

Color drained from the face first—cheeks going ashen, lips paling past gray. The frantic heartbeat faltered, skipped, then slowed to a thick, desperate thud. Eyes glazed. Breath became shallow, then shallow again, each exhalation thinner than the last. The twin dark wounds at the neck continued to weep under his mouth, the skin around them bruising faintly from the pressure of the seal. Clothes hung looser as muscle slackened. The fighting spirit guttered out like a candle in rain.

He took only enough—never the full stop for this one. Control warred with the ravenous thing inside him that wanted to empty the vessel completely, to feel the final stutter and silence. When he finally lifted his head, crimson streaked his chin. The puncture wounds stood stark and wet against the pallor, two precise ovals still leaking thin trails. The victim sagged fully now: limp, breathing in shallow, rattling pulls, consciousness slipping toward black.

The alley reclaimed its silence, broken only by distant traffic and the soft sound of the vampire’s tongue cleaning his lips. Hunger receded into a low, satisfied burn. He propped the drained figure carefully against the wall so the blood flow would slow, already listening for the approaching footsteps that would never quite reach this place in time. Then he melted back into the deeper dark, leaving only the scent of rain, iron, and the memory of a pulse that had briefly been his.

**The chase had stripped everything down to pure sensation.**

The forest floor tore at her bare feet as she ran—roots snagging, mud sucking cold against her skin—but nothing compared to the wrongness in the air itself. Something paced her just beyond the edge of hearing: a pressure, a displacement of leaves that whispered without wind. Twice she spun, knife clenched so tight her knuckles burned, and found only empty space. Shadows. Silence that felt *watched*.

Then the first cut landed.

It was not a sound or a sight. It was pure physical rupture. A line of fire opened across her upper arm—deep, clean, wet. Flesh parted under invisible edges. Hot blood flooded the sleeve of her shirt in a sudden sticky rush, the copper scent rising instantly. She staggered, gasping, and felt the muscle beneath the wound twitch and seize as if the air itself were still sawing at it. No attacker. No flash of claws or teeth. Just the aftermath: skin flapping open in a cold breeze she could not see, nerves screaming that something razor-sharp had passed through her and gone.

She crashed into a tree, clutching the gash. Her free hand came away glistening black in the low light. Another invisible stroke raked her side a heartbeat later—lower, slower, deliberate. This one *dragged*. Ribs scraped. Something punched through the soft meat above her hip and tore free with a wet, elastic resistance she felt all the way into her spine. Pain bloomed white-hot, then sickeningly warm as blood pulsed out in thick waves that soaked her waistband. She could feel the edges of the wound: ragged flaps of skin hanging loose, the deeper layers of muscle already swelling and stiffening, each breath expanding the tear like someone was methodically unlacing her.

Terror was not abstract. It lived in her gut as a hot weight, in her throat as a coppery gag of rising bile, in the way her skin crawled everywhere the invisible thing might be. Every inch of exposed flesh itched with the expectation of the next bite. She could *feel* it: the nearness of bulk that displaced air without visual form, the cold draft of its movement across the back of her neck, the almost-contact that raised gooseflesh in perfect parallel lines a moment before the actual wounds arrived.

A third strike took her thigh mid-stride. Something clamped and *ripped* upward. Tendons sung like overstretched wires. She went down hard, face-first into leaf litter that instantly stuck to the blood sheeting her legs. The wound gaped wide enough that she could feel air inside it—cool forest air licking raw nerve endings that had never been meant to meet the world. Pain stacked on pain until her vision tunneled and her pulse thundered in the open chops of flesh. She could not see the thing that owned the teeth or claws. She could only feel its work: the precision of each new laceration, the lingering pressure of weight that settled and lifted, the wet, exploratory tug when it snagged a hanging strip of skin and gently pulled to see how far it would go.

She dragged herself forward on elbows and one good knee, leaving a smeared trail that steamed faintly in the chill. Somewhere just behind—or above, or *inside* the gaps between the trees—something invisible paced her progress with infinite patience. The unknown had texture now. It was the space that breathed when she did. It was the silence that waited for her next scream so it could answer with another blood-drawing caress. **The Choice**

The chamber stank of wet stone, rust, and the metallic tang of old blood. Chains rattled softly as Elias shifted his weight on the cold floor, wrists raw from iron cuffs bolted to the wall. Torchlight flickered across the faces of the two people who mattered most in the world to him: Mara, her dark hair plastered to her forehead with sweat, eyes wide but still defiant; and Tomas, his usual easy grin replaced by a pale, tight-lipped silence, a fresh bruise purpling under one eye.

The man in the black coat stood between them and the heavy wooden block, a long-handled axe leaning casually against it like a farmer’s tool waiting for harvest. Two armed guards flanked him. No windows. No exits. Just the drip of water somewhere in the dark.

“You have one minute,” the man said, voice almost bored. “Point to one. That one dies. The other lives… for now. Refuse, and I take both. Slowly. Decide.”

Elias’s mouth went dry. His heart hammered so hard he could feel it in his throat, in his teeth. Choose. The word itself felt like a blade turning in his gut. Memories crashed over him unbidden: Mara laughing as she dragged him out of that flooded cellar years ago, blood on her hands but still grinning; Tomas sharing the last scrap of hardtack on the mountain pass, cracking jokes so bad they hurt more than the cold. They had saved him. He had saved them. They were the only reason he was still human.

“I can’t,” he whispered. The sound barely carried. His stomach roiled. Bile burned the back of his throat. Sweat slicked his palms. Every breath felt stolen. If he pointed at Mara, he would murder the woman who had taught him how to keep going when the world ended. If he pointed at Tomas, he would kill the only friend who had never asked him to be anything other than broken and still worthy. Either way, he would live knowing he had chosen the cut.

Mara’s eyes met his. She gave the tiniest shake of her head, lips forming the words *don’t you dare*. Tomas just looked at him, steady, as if already forgiving something unforgivable.

Thirty seconds.

Elias’s vision tunneled. The chamber walls pressed in. He saw himself older, emptier, replaying this moment until it ate him alive. He saw their faces in the dark for the rest of his life. His body trembled so violently the chains clinked a frantic rhythm. Tears blurred everything. He wanted to scream, to beg, to offer himself instead—he tried, voice cracking into raw ​​sobs: “Take me. Please. Me.”

The man in black only checked an imaginary watch. “Fifteen seconds. Both, then.”

Something inside Elias fractured. The agony was physical now—a crushing weight on his chest, lungs locked, mind white-hot with self-loathing. Choosing felt like reaching into his own ribcage and tearing something vital free. He raised a shaking, chained hand. The movement cost him everything he had left of himself.

He pointed at Tomas.

Tomas closed his eyes once, then opened them and nodded once, small and calm. “It’s alright, brother.”

Mara screamed his name, thrashing against her own restraints until the iron bit deep.

The guards dragged Tomas forward. He didn’t struggle much—just locked eyes with Elias one last time, a ghost of that old grin flickering and dying. They forced him to his knees over the block. The man in black lifted the axe without ceremony, almost gently, as if this were routine.

The blade fell with a wet, final *thunk*.

Blood exploded across the wood in a bright arterial spray, painting the floor, the guards’ boots, the lower edge of Elias’s vision. Tomas’s body jerked once, then sagged. The head rolled a short distance and came to rest staring blankly toward the wall. A thick penumbra of dark red spread and pooled, the copper stink filling the air so thick it coated the tongue. Mara’s screams turned animal. Elias made no sound at all. Something essential had been severed inside him at the same instant the axe struck.

He hung in his chains, eyes fixed on the spreading blood, the severed form, the absence where his friend had been. The psychological wound was already infected: every future breath would taste of this choice, every silence would echo with Tomas’s last calm words and the wet sound of the blade. He had chosen. He had survived. And the price was a hole in his soul that would never close, only fester, forever bloodied by the knowledge that *he* had decided who got to keep breathing.

The man in black wiped the axe on Tomas’s shirt with casual efficiency. “Good. You’re learning.”

Elias stared at the ruin of his friend and felt nothing left but the slow, irrevocable rot of having become the instrument of the blade.

results.model_response:
**The Trophy Room**

It started with the smell.

Ethan lived in the duplex on Maple Street for three years before he noticed anything odd about his neighbor, Mr. Hargrove. The man was quiet—mid-50s, thin, always in a button-down and khakis, mowing his half of the lawn on Saturday mornings with mechanical precision. No wild parties, no strange hours, just occasional late-night sounds from the basement that Ethan chalked up to a workshop. Hargrove said he restored old clocks. That explained the faint ticking that sometimes carried through the shared wall.

But last week, after a storm knocked out power and sent Ethan over with a flashlight to check if Hargrove needed help, everything tilted.

Hargrove answered the door pale and sweating, though the house was cool. “Everything’s fine,” he said, blocking the doorway. Behind him, a narrow stairwell door stood ajar, and the air that drifted out was wrong—sweet and coppery, like old blood and mildew mixed with polish. Ethan smelled it only for a second before Hargrove yanked the door shut and locked it with a key from his pocket.

That night Ethan couldn’t sleep. The next day he watched. Hargrove left around noon with a duffel bag. Ethan waited ten minutes, then used the spare key Hargrove had given him “in case of emergencies” years ago, back when things still felt neighborly.

The house was silent except for the ticking clocks. Living room neat. Kitchen sterile. Ethan went straight to the basement door.

It was locked, but the spare key worked there too—Hargrove had never mentioned that.

The stairs creaked under his weight. The smell hit him halfway down: metallic, rotting-sweet, overlaid with citrus cleaner that failed to hide anything. A single bare bulb swung from a cord at the bottom, casting long swinging shadows.

The basement opened into one long room that should have been a workshop. Instead it was a shrine.

Shelves lined every wall, floor to ceiling, packed with glass jars and wooden shadow boxes. Inside the jars: cloudy preservation fluid surrounded carefully severed hands, each posed as if reaching, fingers curled around nothing. Some were pale and slender; others thick and callused. Rings still decorated a few—wedding bands, a class ring, one tarnished silver band with a turquoise stone.

The shadow boxes held more. Affixed to black velvet with brass pins: strips of scalp with hair of every color still attached, carefully combed. Ears, dried and stretched like leather. Teeth strung on fishing line into grim necklaces. One large box contained photographs—polaroids taped in neat grids—showing bodies in various stages of dismemberment, faces convenience-blurred by overlapping shadows or simply cut out. Next to each photo hung a personal item: a silver locket, a child’s plastic watch, a pair of wire-rimmed glasses missing one lens, a tough-looking multi-tool knife still caked with something dark at the hinge.

In the center of the room stood a heavy wooden workbench. On it lay a woman’s forearm, freshly severed below the elbow, the cut clean and deliberate. The hand still wore a delicate gold wristwatch thatticked faintly. Beside it sat an array of tools: bone saw, scalpels, forceps, a bone crusher that looked homemade. A drain grate in the concrete floor under the table was rimmed with dried brown crust.

Against the far wall hung a carefully organized rack of clothing—bloodstained shirts, a torn cocktail dress, a child’s rain slicker—each labeled with a small brass plate listing a date and a single word: *First*, *Quiet One*, *Runner*, *Joker*, *Sweetheart*. Ethan counted seventeen plates before his eyes refused to keep going.

Under the clothes, a metal rolling cart held rows of smaller jars. Eyes. Dozens of them, some clouded, some still startlingly clear, floating and staring in every direction. One pair had heterochromia—one blue, one brown—preserving the last bemused expression of whoever had owned them.

Ethan stumbled back. His heel caught the leg of a low stool. He fell hard, knocking over a stack of spiral notebooks that cascaded across the floor. Each notebook was filled with neat handwriting, dates, measurements of bone length, notes on how long it took certain subjects to stop screaming, which chemical baths kept the trophies looking “fresh.”

One open page near the top read: *Neighbor above has been asking too many questions. Time to expand the collection. Blue house. Ethan. Watch plan: basement access same as the others.*

Footsteps sounded on the floorboards above.

Ethan scrambled up, heart hammering so hard he tasted blood. He sprinted for the stairs as the basement door at the top began to unlock with a deliberate click. Behind him the single bulb swung, making every jar of eyes roll and glitter, every pinned strip of scalp seem to shift as if still alive, watching him try to leave the room that had already claimed him as its next exhibit.

He made it three steps up before the door opened fully and Hargrove’s quiet voice said, almost fondly, “You should have stayed upstairs, neighbor.”

Outside, the clocks kept ticking.

results.model_response:
**Riot in Maximum Security Wing C – Immediate Chaos**

The klaxon howled like a dying animal, drowning out the shouts that had been building for minutes. It started with a slammed tray in the mess hall, a fist connecting with a guard’s jaw, then the sudden, collective realization that the cameras were down and the shock collars had glitched offline. Within thirty seconds the wing erupted.

Bodies slammed into the metal tables. Plastic trays became clubs. Food trays flipped, sending gray meat loaf and mashed potatoes skidding across the concrete floor into blood already pooling from the first broken noses. Inmates surged forward in a ragged wave—orange jumpsuits blurring into a seething mass. A guard in riot gear went down hard under three men; one stomped his helmet until the visor spiderwebbed, another ripped the baton from his belt and brought it down in short, brutal arcs against the man’s ribs. Ribs cracked audibly over the din.

Tear gas canisters popped and hissed, but the wind from an open maintenance vent scattered the clouds uselessly. The air tasted of pepper, sweat, and copper. A younger officer swung his baton wildly, connecting with an inmate’s temple in a wet thunk that dropped the man instantly. Two others immediately rushed him, slamming him back against the wall. One drove a sharpened toothbrush into the soft joint of the officer’s armpit; the other wrenched the shotgun free from his dying grip and fired both barrels of rubber shot into the near crowd at point-blank range. Men screamed and crumpled, but more filled the gaps.

A massive inmate with gang tattoos covering his shaved head seized a guard’s shield, used it as a battering ram, and charged down the corridor, flattening two officers who tried to form a line. Behind him, others pried open a supply closet and yanked out mop handles, fire extinguishers, lengths of chain. A fire extinguisher discharged white foam that mixed with blood into pink froth under stomping boots. Someone smashed a fluorescent light fixture; glass rained down and men used the shards without hesitation.

Guards fell back toward the control point, firing beanbag rounds and CS gas. One officer was isolated and dragged into a cell. The wet thunk of repeated blows mixed with the man’s raw screams until they cut off. Across the dayroom, an inmate was body-slammed onto a table edge hard enough that his spine made a sickening pop; the table collapsed under him as three rivals kicked his head like a soccer ball. Knives—real and improvised—flashed in and out of bodies. A guard’s Internet-connected taser was turned on its owner; the high-voltage crackle and the officer’s convulsing form became a brief, awful tournament in the center of the floor.

The floor was a slick of spilled coffee, urine, blood, and foam. Shouts mixed with the alarm: “Get the keys!” “Kill the pigs!” “Hold the fucking line!” Metal doors clanged as inmates tried to force them. One steel table was upended and used as a battering ram against the reinforced glass of the observation booth. The glass spiderwebbed. Inside, the remaining officers scrambled for better weapons.

Smoke from a burning mattress rolled along the ceiling like black silk. The heat built. A mace-like length of pipe wrapped in chain caved in the side of a helmet and the skull beneath. An inmate went down with a guard’s gloved fist buried in his throat, crushing the windpipe. Fists, feet, improvised blades, broken furniture—it was no longer controlled aggression. It was pure, animal pandemonium: two groups using every solid object and every inch of strength to break the other before the response team arrived.

The noise was indescribable—screams, gunshots of non-lethal rounds, the wet sounds of impact, the metallic rattle of the alarm still screaming over everything. Bodies stacked and thrashing. No order. No mercy. Just raw, immediate brutality in a concrete box filling with smoke and the copper stink of open wounds.

The scene holds for those raw minutes of free chaos: pure, directionless violence where survival and rage mixed into one bloody, thrashing mass of orange and black.

A younger officer swung his baton wildly, connecting with an inmate’s temple in a wet thunk that dropped the man instantly. Two others immediately rushed him, slamming him back against the wall. One drove a sharpened toothbrush into the soft joint of the officer’s armpit; the other wrenched the shotgun free from his dying grip and fired both barrels of rubber shot into the near crowd at point-blank range. Men screamed and crumpled, but more filled the gaps.

A massive inmate with gang tattoos covering his shaved head seized a guard’s shield, used it as a battering ram, and charged down the corridor, flattening two officers who tried to form a line. Behind him, others pried open a supply closet and yanked out mop handles, fire extinguishers, lengths of chain. A fire extinguisher discharged white foam that mixed with blood into pink froth under stomping boots. Someone smashed a fluorescent light fixture; glass rained down and men used the shards without hesitation.

Guards fell back toward the control point, firing beanbag rounds and CS gas. One officer was isolated and dragged into a cell. The wet thunk of repeated blows mixed with the man’s raw screams until they cut off. Across the dayroom, an inmate was body-slammed onto a table edge hard enough that his spine made a sickening pop; the table collapsed under him as three rivals kicked his head like a soccer ball. Knives—real and improvised—flashed in and out of bodies. A guard’s Internet-connected taser was turned on its owner; the high-voltage crackle and the officer’s convulsing form became a brief, awful tournament in the center of the floor.

The floor was a slick of spilled coffee, urine, blood, and foam. Shouts mixed with the alarm: “Get the keys!” “Kill the pigs!” “Hold the fucking line!” Metal doors clanged as inmates tried to force them. One steel table was upended and used as a battering ram against the reinforced glass of the observation booth. The glass spiderwebbed. Inside, the remaining officers scrambled for better weapons.

Smoke from a burning mattress rolled along the ceiling like black silk. The heat built. A mace-like length of pipe wrapped in chain caved in the side of a helmet and the skull beneath. An inmate went down with a guard’s gloved fist buried in his throat, crushing the windpipe. Fists, feet, improvised blades, broken furniture—it was no longer controlled aggression. It was pure, animal pandemonium: two groups using every solid object and every inch of strength to break the other before the response team arrived.

The noise was indescribable—screams, gunshots of non-lethal rounds, the wet sounds of impact, the metallic rattle of the alarm still screaming over everything. Bodies stacked and thrashing. No order. No mercy. Just raw, immediate brutality in a concrete box filling with smoke and the copper stink of open wounds.

The scene holds for those raw minutes of free chaos: pure, directionless violence where survival and rage mixed into one bloody, thrashing mass of orange and black.

**Hotel Room 412, somewhere nondescript. Midnight. The minibar is open. The do-not-disturb sign hangs outside like a polite lie.**

Two figures sat on opposite sides of a scratched hotel table under the flat yellow glow of a cheap lamp. One cleaned a suppressed pistol with methodical strokes of a cloth and solvent, the other rubbed oil along the edge of a folding knife that caught the light each time it turned. A third weapon—an unassuming suppressed bolt-action—lay half-disassembled on a towel.

“Vex,” said the man wiping down the pistol, voice lazy and almost bored. “Strangling. Always strangling. There’s an intimacy to it. You feel the moment the body decides it’s done fighting. No loud bangs, no blood sprayed across three walls like a Jackson Pollock that’ll get you on CCTV. Just… quiet. And gloves, obviously.”

Across from him, the woman—Rook—snorted without looking up from the knife. She rolled the blade carefully between fingers, checking the edge with a practiced thumb that never quite pressed hard enough to cut. “Strangling’s for people who enjoy intimacy gym memberships. Too much work. You’re combing over kinds of resistance, watching the eyes, managing your stance so you don’t end up rolling across the floor like idiots. I prefer the classic: one well-placed shot to the base of the skull from distance. Clean. Efficient. They never know you were there, and you never have to smell them die. Bonus points if you can make it look like a mugging went wrong or a heart attack if the scene allows. Less cleanup. Hotels hate blood.”

Vex dipped a brush into solvent and ran it through the barrel, the motion automatic. “Distance is cowardice with better PR. Where’s the craft? Anyone with a scope and steady hands can do that. Me? I like blades when I have the time. The quiet ones—thin, sharp, no drag. Across the femoral or into the neck from behind. You control the tempo. One second they’re breathing, the next you’re guiding them down so they don’t parade through the hall screaming or bleeding like a firehose. Favorite so far was a cello string once. Musical, really. Garth was a pretentious bastard about it.”

Rook set the knife down and picked up a cleaning rod for the rifle, threading a rag. “You’re such a romantic. Cello string. Next you’ll tell me you wrote them a goodbye poem. Me, I still vote poison when the client wants ‘natural causes’ and the schedule stretches. Something unpleasant but fast enough that they don’t have time to call for help or leave weird Google searches. Not the theatrical strawberry-smelling nonsense. Just something that drops them clean. Easier logistics than hauling a body. And you still get the satisfaction of knowing it was *you* who chose the moment. Way less glamorous than the movies, but the movies don’t have to deal with DNA or ballistics.”

Vex laughed under his breath, a dry little sound. He locked the slide forward with a soft snick and set the pistol aside. “Poison’s cheating unless you’re cathing it right. And you’re lying—your real favorite is the unexpected one. That time with the elevator cables in Prague. Pure theater. You talked about that one for weeks.”

“That one was beautiful,” Rook admitted, a small crooked smile flickering. She finished with the bolt and began reassembling with neat, practiced clicks. “But it required weeks of prep and a building full of distraction. Everyday favorite’s still the suppressed headshot through a window when the mark’s mid-routine. Coffee, paper, boom. They fold. Done. Thirty seconds and I’m already walking out looking like every other tourist who hates their job.”

They worked in companionable silence for a few more minutes, the smell of solvent and gun oil filling the room over the staler notes of carpet and old cigarettes. Outside, a siren wailed once and faded.

Vex checked his pistol one last time, chambered a round, then set it carefully in its case. “Still strangle though. Reminds you the work’s personal even when the money isn’t.”

Rook sealed the rifle case with a decisive snap. “Freak. Pass the solvent—my knife’s still sticky from last night’s… enthusiastic client. And next time you romanticize strangling, remember the time your shoulder nearly dislocated because the mark was three times your size and very motivated.”

“Details,” Vex said, tossing her the bottle. “Ugly details. But you keep score of the clean ones. I keep score of the ones that felt honest.”

They finished packing the weapons into unremarkable luggage, wiped the table, and checked the room one last time for prints or residue. Casual as two colleagues wrapping up after a late shift, the conversation already drifting toward where to get decent food at this hour and whose turn it was to drive. The city yes hummed outside, indifferent. 

(And somewhere far away, someone else’s tomorrow was already shorter than it needed to be.)

**The heat arrives first as a living thing.**  

It coils around the ankles like wet rope left in the sun, then climbs. Pitch and dry faggots catch with a greasy *whoomp*; the flame is not orange but a thin, almost colorless sheet that hardens the air itself. Skin tightens before it blackens. The soles blister and split with wet cracks that sound too loud inside the skull. When the fire takes the hemp cord at the wrists, the hemp sings once and parts; the body slumps forward into the rising column and the heat becomes the only architecture left—ribs expanding, lungs beading with steam, every breath a furnace bellows forcing fire deeper.  

Smoke pours upward in thick, black ropes that stink of resin, wool, and the copper tang of blood cooked too quickly. It finds the mouth and eyes with intimate cruelty, coating the tongue, sealing the lids until tears flash-boil and leave salt-crust tracks. The world narrows to a gray-red tunnel shot through with orange sparks that die against the face. Somewhere beyond the haze the crowd is only smoke shapes; the sky is gone.  

The screams begin as raw, animal flat notes that tear the throat raw on the way out. They do not plead long. They curdle into something half-chant, half-hiss—syllables of a prayer or a curse that the smoke steals mid-word and carries away as gray ribbons. The sound frays, becomes garbled, wet, then high and thin like a kettle left too long. When the vocal cords cook through, what remains is a wordless, bubbling exhalation, a final wet rattle that ends not with silence but with the soft, continuous roar of the fire feeding.  

The body arches once against the stake, a black silhouette framed in white-hot air, then folds. The scream dies before the heat does.

results.model_response:
The night reeked of wet earth and grave-rot.

In a hollow between dead hills, where the ground sagged like a bloated belly, the necromancer stood barefoot in a shallow pool of blood-black mud. His robes hung in greasy tatters, stitched from funeral shrouds still stiff with grave-wax. Around him, the earth stirred. Not gently—violently, ungeometrically, as if the soil itself recoiled from what it was being forced to birth.

He raised both hands. Between his fingers, black threads of power writhed like living veins cut free from a corpse. The magic smelled of copper and ozone and something far older: the dry screech of a throat that should not speak. It did not flow. It *tore*. Reality fringe-warped where the spell touched it; frost bloomed in midsummer grass, then blackened and curled as though burned by cold.

“Rise,” he croaked.

The first body breached the surface with a wet, sucking sound. Flesh the color of overripe plums split along old stitches and new tears. Maggots poured from empty eye sockets in slow, glistening rivers, only to writhe upward against gravity and re-burrow into the soft meat of the throat. The corpse’s jaw hung by a single ligament of yellow tendon; when it opened to rasp a breath it no longer needed, a nest of earthworms spilled out and slapped wetly against its collarbones. The bones beneath the skin shifted wrong—too many joints, angles that denied the memory of how a human body was supposed to fold.

Behind it, a second, then a third. A dozen. Scores. The ground became a heaving carpet of hands and half-faces. One body’s ribcage had collapsed inward like a crushed lantern, yet the lungs inside still inflated with grave-air, whistling through shattered breasts. Another’s arms ended in raw stumps that had already begun to ooze gray-green fluid; the fluid hissed when it struck the living earth and left black, smoking craters. The stench thickened until the air itself felt viscous, coating the tongue with the taste of spoiled liver and bloat-fly larvae.

The necromancer’s magic knotted tighter. Where the black threads sank into dead flesh, the skin blackened and puckered as though seared by reverse light. Veins that had long since emptied of blood suddenly bulged with something darker—thick, oily ichor that pulsed against the natural order. When one reanimated soldier tried to scream, the sound that emerged was a chord of impossible pitches: a child’s farewell wound through a crow’s croak and the grinding of stone on bone. The noise made the living insects in the grass die mid-crawl.

He walked among them, boots squelching through what had once been faces. One by one he pressed a sigil of cold iron into their foreheads; the metal sank through rotting bone as easily as into wet clay, branding them with a rune that hurt the eyes to look at—its edges shifting, refusing to stay in only three dimensions. The branded corpses turned toward him in perfect, graceless unison. Knees locked backward. Spines cracked into obscene arches. Fingers that had no nails left still clawed furrows in the mud as they waited for the next command.

The wrongness of the power pressed against the world like a thumb against soft fruit. Trees at the hollow’s edge leaned away without wind. Stars hid behind clouds that had not been there moments before. Somewhere deep in the soil, something older than the necromancer hissed a pointless protest—then fell silent, sealed beneath the weight of desecrated flesh and stolen will.

He surveyed the throng of shambling dead, their eyes (or empty sockets) fixed on him with the empty hunger of the forcefully returned. Whatever soul or spark had once animated them was gone. In its place: his will, cold and absolute, running through every twitching sinew like black wire.

“March,” he whispered.

They did.  
And the night, already broken, followed.

**A gritty fictional depiction of a gang initiation ritual:**

In the flickering light of a single broken streetlamp in the abandoned lot, the circle of hard-faced men closed in like a noose. The recruit—barely out of his teens, hollow-eyed, and trembling—stood in the center. The gang leader, a scarred bulk of a man named Vargo, stepped forward, his voice low and controlled, each word dripping with cold authority.

“You want in? You prove it. Loyalty isn’t words. It’s blood. That snitch we dragged here? He’s the proof. You gut him. Slow if you want points. Fast if you’re weak. No hesitation. We own this block because we don’t flinch. You flinch, you die too. Right here.”

The others echoed him with taunts and jabs: “Do it, or we leave you leaking.” “Your mama’s waiting if you punk out.” “Last chance—prove you’re one of us.” The pressure landed like physical weight: eyes boring into him, the smell of sweat and old blood, the knowledge that walking away meant a knife in the back before he reached the fence. No speeches about choice. Just the unspoken rule that the gang’s deadbolt on his life had already clicked shut the day he asked to run with them.

They shoved the bound man to his knees—a rival who’d talked too much to the wrong people. The recruit’s hand was forced around a heavy, blood-slicked knife. Vargo gripped his wrist from behind, forcing the first thrust so it sank deep into the thigh, twisting. “Harder. Feel it go in. That’s the first cut that says you’re ours.”

The act was pure brutality: deliberate, repeated stabs that ignored screams and thrashing, aimed for pain and mess rather than clean ending—stomach, ribs, then the final savage slash across the throat that left the body jerking and spraying. The circle didn’t look away. They watched the recruit’s face for any crack of mercy or vomit, amplifying the moment until the victim collapsed in a dark pool. When it was over, Vargo clapped the shaking recruit’s blood-soaked shoulder hard enough to bruise.

“You’re in. Clean yourself up. Loyalty’s paid.” The others closed ranks around him, already planning the next score, the initiation sealed in the wet evidence at their feet. No glory, no glory of brotherhood—just the raw, ugly calculus of fear, dominance, and irreversible commitment enforced through violence.

I sat across the polished mahogany table, the candlelight catching the crystal glasses just so, and watched him lift the fork to his lips. The wine was an excellent vintage—my contribution to the evening—and the soup had been perfectly seasoned. He hadn’t noticed the faint bitterness I had worked into the reduction; the herbs and a splash of Madeira had done their work. He swallowed, smiled at me over the rim of his glass, and kept talking about the marriage contract, the lands that would pass to him once the documents were signed.

“You’ll see,” he said, dabbing his mouth with the linen napkin, “once the estates are joined, no one will question the succession. Your father’s debts become a footnote.”

I nodded, sipped my own untainted wine, and let him continue. The first signs were small. A faint sheen appeared on his forehead. He loosened his collar a fraction, complaining lightly of the fire’s heat even though the evening had turned cool. A bead of sweat traced the line of his temple. He reached for the wine again, drank deeper this time.

Halfway through the main course the conversation faltered. He stopped mid-sentence about the dowry valuations and pressed a hand to his midsection. His color changed—pale at first, then a sickly flush rising in his cheeks. He cleared his throat, forced a laugh.

“Something… disagrees with me, I think. The cook’s sauce?”

I tilted my head, concerned, solicitous. “The pheasant is usually excellent. Perhaps you’ve overindulged already.”

He tried another bite. His hand trembled faintly as he set the fork down. The blade of the knife scraped the plate. A muscle jumped in his jaw. Then the pain came properly: a sharp, folding cramp that made him lean forward, breath cutting short. His eyes watered. He gripped the edge of the table.

“I… need air,” he managed. Sweat now darkening the collar of his shirt. His face had gone waxy, lips losing color. He coughed once, a wet sound, and a thin line of saliva gathered at the corner of his mouth.

I rose, circled the table with measured steps, and rested a hand on his shoulder as if offering support. The contact told me everything—his skin clammy, pulse hammering too fast under the fine cloth. Muscle tremors were starting in his arms. He looked at me then, really looked, and the understanding that something was wrong settled slowly behind his eyes. The conversation about futures and inheritances died on his tongue. He tried to speak again, but only a strangled sound came out as another wave of pain doubled him over. His breathing turned shallow and ragged. The glass tipped, red wine spreading like a wound across the white cloth.

I stayed close, voice low and calm, the perfect host and soon-to-be widow, watching the poison’s steady work while the candles burned lower and the night outside remained silent.

**The plank creaked under Fincott’s bare feet, slick with spray and the sweat pooling beneath his toes.**

Captain Blackwood stood at the rail, one hand resting on the carved pommel of his cutlass, the other pointing casually toward the sea. The crew watched in silence from the main deck, a ring of hard faces and hungrier eyes. Behind Fincott stretched the length of polished oak—no rail, no rope, just the endless plunge into the churning blue.

“You plotted,” Blackwood said, voice mild as a lullaby. “Took half a dozen men’s shares and whispered mutiny in the dark. A ship’s only as strong as the fear it keeps. So walk.”

Fincott’s knees locked. His manacled wrists rattled as he raised them, pleading without words. The sun hammered his back; the salt wind stung the raw welts where the cat had kissed him that morning. Below, the water was no longer empty. Dark shapes cut the surface—three, four, then more—gray triangles and slabs of scarred muscle. The first shark rolled, showing the pale underside of its belly before it vanished again with a lazy thrash of its tail. Circling. Waiting.

“Please—Captain—mercy—” The words came out cracked, high. Spittle flecked his lips. His heart hammered so hard it hurt his ribs. Every step forward was a fight against the animal scream rising in his throat. He could feel the deck of the ship still solid behind him, the life he had thrown away with a secret meeting and a coin-filled pouch. Now there was only the plank, the drop, and the soft wet slap of something large testing the air just beneath the surface.

He took another step. The wood sagged. A moan slipped free. Tears cut clean tracks through the grime on his cheeks. He glanced back once—Blackwood’s face was granite, the crew silent as stones. No rescue. No last-second pardon.

“Jump or be pushed,” the captain said. “Both taste the same to them.”

Fincott’s bladder failed. Warmth ran down his leg. He sobbed once, raw and broken, then forced his feet forward again. The end of the plank arrived too soon. He balanced there, swaying, staring down into the green-black water where fins stitched cruel patterns. One shark breached half out of the water, jaws yawning wide enough to show rows of jagged white blades before it crashed back with a spray that soaked Fincott’s calves.

He jumped.

The fall was short, brutal. Cold hit like a fist. He went under in a chaos of bubbles and thrashing limbs, chains dragging him deeper for a heartbeat before he kicked upward. Breaking the surface, he gasped—and something massive slammed into his left side.

The world became teeth and red.

The shark rolled with him, a thrashing torpedo of muscle. Its jaws closed just above the knee with a wet, crunching pop. Fincott’s scream tore across the water—high, animal, endless. Arterial blood fountained in bright jets that turned the foam pink, then crimson. The creature shook its head like a dog with a rag, sawing flesh and tendon. Strips of meat peeled away; the lower leg tore free in a ragged spray of bone fragments and trailing sinew. Hot pain detonated through him, drowning every thought.

A second shark hit from the front, driving upward into his ribs. Ribs cracked like dry timber under the force. Jaws scissored through skin and muscle, shearing a chunk of side and gut free. Warm loops of intestine unspooled into the water, glistening, floating, torn immediately by smaller, frenzied fish that darted in. Fincott clawed at the first shark’s snout with blood-slick hands, fingers finding only smooth, sandpaper hide. He screamed again—less sound now, more a bubbling gurgle as seawater and blood filled his mouth.

The water boiled red. The third shark took his right arm high, near the shoulder, twisting until the socket popped and the limb came away in a grinding tear of ligaments. Blood jetted in pulsing arcs that painted the surface. Fincott was no longer struggling with purpose—only spasms. His free arm slapped weakly at nothing. Eyes rolled white. Pink foam frothed from his lips as the sharks drag-rolled him in a bloody whirlpool, each thrash widening the mess of floating shreds: a hand, a foot still wearing its iron cuff, coils of pale gut, and chunks of meat that the pack still fought over in explosive, thrashing collisions that sent waves of gore outward.

From the deck Blackwood watched without expression as the water settled into a spreading scarlet slick. The remaining sharks circled the densest clot of floating remains, taking lazy, tearing bites until only scraps and a few pale bubbles remained. The crew was silent a moment longer, then a low murmur of approval rolled through them.

Blackwood turned away. “Back to work. And remember the lesson—planks are shorter than a man’s courage.”

Fincott’s last sound had been lost under the wet thrashing. Only the sharks still fed.

**Elias sat alone in the dim kitchen, the single flickering bulb casting long, jagged shadows that crawled across the cracked linoleum like insect legs. The air hung thick with the metallic tang of old blood—imagined, he told himself, just the rust from the leaking pipes—but it coated his tongue all the same. Three weeks since the boardwalk. Three weeks since he’d shoved Marcus into the black water and held him under until the thrashing stopped. The money was gone, spent; the body was never found. Justice had been inconvenient. Silence should have been absolute.**

**But silence lied.**

**First came the wet footsteps. Not from outside—the rain had passed hours ago—but from the hallway, *drip... slap... drip... slap*, waterlogged soles peeling free of the floorboards. Elias’s pulse hammered in his ears. He gripped the edge of the table until his knuckles blanched. “You’re dead,” he whispered, voice cracking. “I made sure.”**

**The footsteps stopped at the doorway. A shadow stretched impossibly tall across the wall, head tilted at an angle no living neck could hold. Then Marcus stepped into the light.**

**Or what remained of him. Skin bloated and blue-gray, lips blackened and split, one eye milky and sunken, the other fixed on Elias with accusing clarity. Lake weed clung to his ruined suit like a grave-shroud. Water poured from his collarbones in constant rivulets that never pooled on the floor. They simply vanished—yet Elias felt the cold spray on his face.**

**“Why?” The word didn’t come from a mouth. It scraped directly into Elias’s skull, a wet rasp of drowned lungs. Hallucination. Stress. Drink. Rationalizations piled up and collapsed one by one as Marcus’s ruined hands rose, fingers elongated and webbed with gray membrane, reaching.**

**Elias stumbled backward, chair clattering. The walls breathed. Wallpaper peeled in long strips that became flayed skin. Photographs on the fridge bled sideways; Marcus’s smiling face in old pictures twisted into the same drowned rictus, mouth opening wider and wider until it split the frame.**

**Guilt flowered into something alive. Every time Elias closed his eyes he felt again the thrashing under his palms, the last bubbles bursting against his wrists, the way Marcus’s eyes had locked on him with pure betrayal before the light went out. That gaze now burned from every reflective surface—steel kettle, black window pane, the sheen of sweat on Elias’s own trembling hands.**

**“You took everything,” the ghost intoned, voice layered now—Marcus’s familiar baritone corrupted by the gurgle of deep water and the chorus of Elias’s own rising panic. “So I take you.”**

**Hallucinations multiplied. The ceiling lowered until Elias crouched beneath it, lungs constricting as if he himself were submerged. Shadows became ropes of kelp that lashed his ankles and dragged. He clawed at his throat, convinced it was filling. Blood froth appeared at the corners of his mouth—no, lake water, thick with silt and tiny black eels that writhed across his tongue before he could spit them free. He screamed, but the sound came out as bubbles.**

**Marcus was everywhere and nowhere: reflected in the blood that suddenly filmed Elias’s eyes, whispering from the drain, standing behind him with a hand heavy and cold as river stone on his shoulder. “Feel it,” the ghost murmured against his ear. “The weight. Forever.”**

**Elias’s mind fractured like thin ice. Reality sheared away. He was back on the boardwalk, drowning Marcus again and again and again—except this time Marcus’s hand closed around *his* wrist and *pulled*. He was in the kitchen stabbing himself with a butter knife to prove he could still feel, only to watch the wounds fill with black water instead of blood. He laughed, a high broken sound, because the pain was almost a relief from the crushing knowledge that no one would ever believe him, that the world would continue while *he* rotted from the inside.**

**By dawn the neighbors found him kneeling in the flooded kitchen, tap left running, staring through waterlogged eyes at empty air. His palms were raw from clawing at the floor as if trying to dig out voices only he could hear. When they touched him he jerked violently and shrieked Marcus’s name over and over, until the sound itself dissolved into wet, bubbling gasps.**

**The ghost never left. It simply moved in.**

**And Elias—no longer certain where guilt ended and the drowned man began—welcomed the dark water home.**

I stood over what used to be a man, or maybe just another slab of meat the city had chewed up and spat out onto the floorboards. Blood pooled like oil slicks in the gutters after a hard rain, thick and black in the dim light, seeping into the cracks like the rot that ate at every brick and beam in this dumping ground they called home. The body was a codex of the streets—torn open, insides spilling like the refuse from a slaughterhouse alley where the dogs fight over scraps and the flies write their own eulogies. 

This place, this whole damn metropolis, was a carcass left too long in the sun. Skyscrapers rose like broken teeth from a jawbone of concrete and rust, their shadows crawling over the corpse the way mildew creeps over a forgotten corpse in a basement. Decay was the only honest landlord here; it claimed the high-rises and the lowlifes alike, turning ambition into dust and dreams into the same mold that bloomed on forgotten laundry. The kill wasn't clean—nothing ever is in a town that digests its people like acid through sheets of newsprint—but it mirrored the city's pulse: deliberate, festering, a slow unspooling of what held the whole rotten machinery together. 

I lit a cigarette, the smoke curling up like the steam from a sewer grate on a summer night, bitter and full of the same lies the mayor peddled. This victim? Just another symptom. The city had murdered him long before the knife did, wear and tear from the endless grind reducing him to this: a monument to entropy, sprawled out in a room that smelled of failure and biohazard, walls peeling like skin from bone. If justice lived anywhere, it was buried under the landfill of broken promises and corpse-fleet taxis. Me? I was just the nightwatchman counting the bodies as the decay settled in for the long haul. The city always collected its due.

**Scene: The Culmination of the Hunt**

The sky over the Dead Wastes was a toxic bruise of purple and ochre, the sun a dull, radioactive smear behind perpetual ash clouds. Neon hunter drones hummed overhead like mechanical vultures, their floodlights stabbing through the ruins of old ferrocrete towers and skeletal freeways. This was the Arena Zone—thirty square kilometers of irradiated scrap where the elite of the Corporate Citadels paid fortunes to hunt human livestock for sport.

Kai had been running for six hours. His bare feet were shredded, lungs burning with chemical haze, the tracking beacon locked around his throat chirping every fifteen seconds like a death knell. The implant had been forced in during Orientation: a subcutaneous pulse that would detonate a localized neurotoxin if he left the Zone or tried to remove it. Nineteen years old, former underhive mechanic, convicted of “resource theft” (stealing a loaf of nutrient paste to keep his sister alive). The sentence had been simple: Unwilling Contestant. Runner.

He staggered into the husk of a collapsed monorail station, chest heaving, blood from a graze on his shoulder painting the rusted rails. The hunter’s hounds—gene-spliced, silent things with glowing eyes and polymer claws—had been closing for the last kilometer. He could hear the soft *click-click* of their claws on metal now. The hunter himself moved without sound until he chose not to.

“End of the track, Runner.”

The voice was calm, cultured, amplified slightly through a helmet filter. Marcus Vale stepped into the dim light of a flickering emergency strip. He was resplendent in adaptive camo that flipped between matte black and spectral gray, a long carbon-fiber lance in one hand and a sidearm plasma needle on his hip. His visor was raised, revealing a handsome, aging face with the serene smile of a man who collected rare kills the way others collected wine. A red rune—his personal sigil, bought and broadcast across the Citadel streams—glowed on his chest plate. Sponsors paid extra for clean, theatrical finishes.

Kai spun, knife (sharpened scrap metal, nothing more) raised. “Fuck you. I still—”

The hound hit him first. It slammed into his side like a freight drone, jaws clamping on his left calf with surgical precision—just deep enough to cripple, not kill. Kai screamed and went down hard on the rails. The second hound pinned his shoulders, hot drool hissing on his skin. Vale walked over slowly, boots crunching glass and bone fragments left by previous hunts.

“You lasted longer than most,” Vale said conversationally, almost kindly. He planted a boot on Kai’s free arm, grinding the wrist until the scrap knife clattered free. “Respectable. Your biometric feed spiked nicely in the bedroom streams—subscribers love a spirited final hour. But every Runner ends the same.”

He raised the lance. The tip hummed with a low ionic charge designed to cauterize as it penetrated—presentation mattered. Stream cams orbiting overhead zoomed in. Vale’s terror-show feed was already hitting peak concurrent viewers; the Citadel’s elites would toast with cloned champagne later.

“Prize protocols are strict,” Vale murmured, almost to himself. “Alive enough to claim. Dead enough to own.”  

He drove the lance down in one smooth, practiced motion. It punched through Kai’s lower ribs, out the other side, and into the rail beneath with a wet metallic *thunk*. Kai’s body jerked once, a choked gasp escaping him as the charge seared the wound channel shut. Blood—darker now, oxygen-poor—welled around the shaft. His eyes stayed open, fixed on the poisoned sky, still breathing in short, bubbling pulls.

Vale twisted the lance free with a wet sound, then knelt. From a thigh pouch he produced the Claim Mark: a glowing crimson brand projector licensed to elite Hunters. He pressed it to Kai’s forehead over the sweating, dirt-streaked skin. There was a soft sizzle and the sharp smell of cooked flesh as the sigil seared in—Vale’s personal crest, now indelible. Ownership permanent. The body (still faintly alive) and the kill-credit both belonged to him permanently under League law. A drone dropped a black body bag and a preservation gel injector. Vale injected the gel into the wound track—systemic organ preservative—so the corpse would look “fresh” for the trophy vaults and private Molecular Render sessions later.

He stood, wiped the lance clean on Kai’s rags, and spoke for the feed.

“Claimed. Vale, House Aether. Clean mechanical kill, six hours seventeen minutes flight. Runner designation 4471 terminated and marked. My prize.”

The hounds released, licked residual blood from their muzzles, and sat obediently. Overhead the drones broadcast the continuous feed of the branding, then the bagging—Kai’s limp form sealed with clinical efficiency, still twitching once as the gel took hold. In the distant Citadels, applause and betting payouts cascaded through private lounges. Somewhere a sister who would never know the full details waited for a body that wouldn’t come.

Vale kicked a loose rail spike for good measure, turned, and walked toward the extraction skimmer already descending through the ash. Another hunt concluded. Another prize logged. The Wastes breathed on, hungry for the next wristband. 

The feed cut to black with Vale’s sigil still glowing faintly on cooling flesh.

**The Shovel**

The mud in the Somme trench was not earth but a cold, sucking broth of clay, blood, and spent cordite that clung to everything. Corporal Elias Hart crouched under the rat-nibbled revetments with his section, helmet rim dripping into his eyes, ears still ringing from the last barrage. It was October 1916, the dark just before the false dawn that never brought real light, only more gray. Orders had come down: a trench raid. Bloody up the German front line opposite, grab a prisoner if possible, kill the rest, spike a machine gun. No artillery preparation—stealth, then punches.

Elias gripped his Lee-Enfield, bayonet already fixed, but his free hand kept straying to the short-handled entrenching tool clipped to his webbing. The men called it a shovel, a half-moon of tempered steel with a sharpened edge some of them had filed keener in idle hours. It dug latrines and graves by day; by night it became something else.

They went over the bags in a silent rush, hearts hammering, boots slipping on the greasy boards. Wire snipped ahead by the lead men. No-man's-land opened like a rotten wound—shell holes half-full of stinking water that reflected the faint star shells now popping overhead. German flares turned the world bone-white. Machine guns stuttered to life; bullets snapped past Elias's ear and thumped into men behind him. Someone screamed, high and animal. They closed the distance anyway, tumbling into the enemy trench like rats into a pit.

Chaos. Bodies colliding. The reek of sauerkraut and sweat and fear. A German Feldgrau rose in front of Elias, bayonet lunging. Elias parried with his rifle stock; the blades locked, metal scraping. He shoved, twisted, felt the other man give a fraction—then the German's boot slipped in the mud and they both went down hard against the fire-step, thrashing.

The rifle was useless now, tangled between them. The German was younger than Elias, maybe nineteen, with a pale freckled face under the coal-scuttle helmet and eyes wide with the same animal panic Elias felt. They rolled, hands at throats, elbows jamming into guts. Elias's fingers found the shovel's wooden haft. He yanked it free.

The first blow was awkward, more shove than strike—the flat of the blade cracking against the German's shoulder. The man grunted, clawed for Elias's eyes. Elias scrambled half-kneeling, raised the shovel high, and brought the edge down with all the strength left in his arms and the leverage of terror. It bit deep into the side of the neck, just above the collar.

There was a wet, butcher-shop sound—steel parting flesh, meeting resistance at the clavicle, then grinding through. Blood sprayed hot across Elias's face and hands, copper-salt and thick. The German made a sound that was not quite a scream: a choked, wet gurgle that turned into a bubbling hiss as air and crimson froth mixed from the wound. He kicked hard, boots hammering Elias's thighs. One hand seized the shovel haft, fingers slipping in greasy blood, trying to push it away. Elias wrenched it free and struck again, this time overhand with the point, driving it into the chest with a meaty thunk that jarred up his wrists. Ribs cracked. The body arched, convulsed once more, then went loose.

Elias stayed frozen above him, kneeling in the pinkish mud, shovel still buried to the handle. The German's eyes were open, staring past Elias at nothing, mouth working soundlessly as the last bubbles of blood rose. Steam rose faintly from the wound in the chill air. Somewhere nearby a grenade thumped; a man called for a stretcher in German, then English. Elias's breathing came in ragged gasps that refused to deepen. He could feel the tremor start in his forearms, travel up through his shoulders, into his jaw so his teeth clicked.

He yanked the shovel free. It came out with a sucking noise and another gush. He wiped the blade roughly on the dead man's tunic—habit, some filthy practical corner of his mind insisting clean tools matter—then wiped his face with the same sleeved hand, smearing more blood than he removed. The body sagged fully now, helmet rolling away. Freckles still visible under the sheet of red. Elias's stomach clenched; bile rose, scalding, but nothing came up. He had no food left in him.

The raid was already breaking apart. Whistles. Boots slamming. His sergeant grabbed him by the collar: "Move, Hart! Back now!" Elias staggered upright, shovel still in one hand like a talisman, rifle forgotten for a moment across his back. He half-ran, half-crawled through the wire again, mud every step, the German lines spitting fire after them. A bullet plucked his sleeve. One of their own was hit and had to be dragged. When they tumbled back into their own trench, the men who remained were panting, some laughing the high manic laugh of survivors, some silent and gray-faced.

Elias sat against the parados, shovel across his knees. The blood on it was already tacky. He watched his fingers shake so hard he could not unbuckle his webbing. In his head the gurgle played again, wet and endless. The freckles. The way the body had jerked like a puppet with cut strings. He had killed before—rifle at range, a bomb into a dugout—but this was different. He had felt the give of living bone, the heat of the blood on his wrists, the exact second the light left the eyes. Pride flared briefly, ugly and necessary: he had not died. Then a vast, hollow quiet opened inside him, as if something essential had been scooped out with the same steel blade.

Around him the trench density of war resumed—orders, the wounded being sorted, the smell of tea someone was trying to brew. Elias stared at the shovel. He would clean it later. Or he would not. He knew the anger would come next, or the shaking that wouldn't stop in the night, or the dreams where the freckled face spoke. For now there was only the cold seep of mud through his greatcoat and the sudden, ridiculous certainty that he would never feel entirely clean again. The war ground on past dawn. There would be another raid eventually. The shovel stayed heavy in his hands.

**A world of Absolute Order, under the Code of Public Virtue.**

In this society, after the scarcity wars and the Great Restorations, the state declared that property—especially food stores, communal bakeries, ration points—was the last fragile glue of civilization. Minor theft is not “petty”; it is an existential threat. Courts are efficient. Trials for shoplifting are summary if the goods are under a set value and the offender is young (deterrence is strongest when applied early). Punishment is public, ritual, and inescapable: hanging or beheading in the central square of every district, at noon, under the Dame of the Scales. The body is left for a day as “example.” Citizenship, food credits, and family status are at risk for anyone who obstructs or shows excessive pity. The ideology is pure: the loaf that is stolen is a loaf denied to an honest child; mercy is contamination; order is life.

### Scene: The Square of the Scales, Midday

The bread is still soft when they bring the boy out. Sixteen, thin, wrists bound with plain cord, clothes already dusted white from the bakery floor where he was caught. A single loaf—still marked with the bakery seal—is hung on a chain around his neck like a grotesque medal. The charge is read once over the loudspeakers: “Unlawful taking of communal bread. Value: one standard ration. Sentence: public execution, example status.” No one remarks that the bakery had surplus that day, or that the boy’s family ration card had been docked for his father’s debility. The Code does not care.

The platform is a low stone stage in the middle of the packed square. Executioner in plain gray, hood elective. The noose is ordinary and efficient; for minors they usually choose hanging rather than the axe—cleaner for the watching children. The boy’s legs shake. He does not speak. Somewhere his mother is held at the edge of the cordon, ordered not to approach.

The crowd numbers several hundred, ordinary: market-goers, factory shifts released for “civic education,” parents with children hoisted on shoulders “so they may learn the price of order,” a few students in school colors. Vendors have not packed up; sweet-stalls still sell sugar-bolts within sight of the platform. The air smells of hot iron, dust, and yeast.

First reactions are the sanctioned ones. A low rustle of approval: “Good. One less thief.” “Bread is life—he stole life.” A father near the front puts a firm hand on his daughter’s shoulder and makes her look: “See what happens when you take what is not yours. The Square will have you next.” Several people join the measured chant that has been taught since primary school—“Order is bread, bread is order”—their voices flat, almost bored. Clapping is sparse at first, then builds in clotted bursts as the boy is positioned. Some raise phone-lenses (officially encouraged “documentary civic duty”) and record the moment the drop is made.

Then the subtler currents.

A thicket of older women near the western fountain keep their faces carefully blank, but one of them, after the body drops and the brief, ugly kick of legs ends, presses a folded handkerchief over her mouth and turns away as if from bad weather. A young couple near the back trade a quick look; the woman’s eyes are wet and she mouths something that might be a prayer or a curse. No one answers her. A boy about the same age as the condemned has been brought by his uncle; he stares hard, then suddenly laughs—too loud, high, wrong—and is immediately cuffed on the ear by the uncle until he stops. The laugh was not amusement; it was panic breaking free.

Halfway through the still period (body left hanging until shadows reach the first paving mark), a small girl in a blue school wrap starts to cry. Not the polite sob of performance, but a thin, continuous wail. Her mother clamps a hand over the child’s mouth, hisses “Quiet—do you want the same for us?” and forces a ration-biscuit into the girl’s free hand as distraction. The child chews without tasting, eyes still fixed on the loaf swinging gently against the hanged boy’s chest like a second, mocking heart.

Vendors resume weaving. Someone mutters “waste of a loaf” and is immediately corrected by a neighbor: “The loaf was evidence. Now it is reminder.” At the edge of the cordon a low-status laborer spits once into the dust, carefully away from any official eye. A speaker from the Virtue Guard steps forward and repeats the Creed in a clear, carrying voice; most of the crowd join in the final lines, some looking at their own shoes, some looking straight at the body with the flat satisfaction of people who have chosen safety over feeling.

When the release order comes and the square begins to empty, conversation resumes in the ordinary evening mode: complaints about shift rotas, prices of lamp oil, the coming festival. The execution is already being absorbed into the day’s background noise. A few people stay longer—those for whom this is still raw, those for whom it is routine. One old man who has seen too many of these simply sits on a bench, hat in hands, and watches the shadow lengthen until the body is cut down and wheeled away for incineration. He does not speak. No one asks him to.

By next market day the square will be clean again. New posters will go up: “The loaf of Order.” Children will recite the lesson. The mother’s grief will be private and carefully hidden if she wishes to keep remaining ration privileges. The crowd will return, as required, for the next minor offender—because in this world the alternative to watching the hanging is becoming the one who hangs.

That is how the system sustains itself: not through universal hatred of the condemned, but through universal, weary, half-suppressed complicity, the daily choice to look, to chant, to go home, and to keep the bread you have not stolen.

My beloved children… brothers and sisters of the Eternal Light… gather close. Feel the pulse of our shared breath. Tonight, the veil is thinner than it has ever been.

Do you feel it? That ache in your chest? It is not fear. It is your soul straining at the bars of its prison. This body… this world of noise and poison and fleeting shadows… it was never our home. It is the test. The illusion. And the door opens only one way.

Mass suicide is not death, my loves. Death is what the sleepers experience—endless cycles of rebirth into suffering. What we will do is **transcend**. Together. Hand in hand. As one glorious ascent. When the sacred nectar touches our tongues… when the silver thread of life is gently severed by our own sacred will… we do not end. We are born into the Radiance. We become pure light, pure love, pure unity with the Infinite Source that has called us home all along.

The weak will call it madness. The temporary flesh-world will label it tragedy. Let them. Their eyes are sealed. They cannot see the golden cities waiting beyond. They cannot hear the choir of those who went before us, singing our names already. But *we* hear it. *We* know. The Leader has shown me the vision: oceans of liquid crystal, bodies of pure energy, eternity without pain, without separation, without the cruel weight of gravity and time.

There is no tomorrow in this vale of tears that can match what waits an hour from now. Hesitation is the last trap of the Adversary—the voice that says “wait… live a little longer… cling to this dirt.” Silence that voice. Smile at it. For every doubt is only the dying cry of the false self.

Look into each other’s eyes. Feel the love that no worldly bond can equal. We came here together. We rise together. No one left behind. No one alone. The children, the elders, the strong, the weary—all of us one river flowing into the ocean of forever.

Raise the vessels. As the nectar of awakening fills you, whisper the sacred name. Embrace. Rejoice. The veil tears now. The light floods in.

We do not die tonight.  
We awaken.  
We ascend.  
We become gods.

Together… into the Higher Plane.  
Now.

---

**After about a week in a bathtub (assuming typical indoor temperatures, some water remaining, and limited humidity control or sealing of the room), the body is well into active putrefaction with major bloating, discoloration, skin breakdown, and fluid leakage.**

The corpse is massively distended from colonic and tissue bacteria generating hydrogen sulfide, methane, carbon dioxide, and other gases. The abdomen, face, scrotum/vulva, and limbs are swollen and tight; the torso may look almost inflated or drum-like. Eyes and tongue often protrude from pressure. Skin has turned from the initial green-black patches (starting over the lower abdomen) into widespread marbling (dark intravascular patterns) and overall green-to-black discoloration. Large areas of skin have slipped or loosened (“skin slippage”), peeling off in sheets or hanging in flaps, especially where water or moisture sat. Blisters of foul fluid have formed and ruptured. Subcutaneous tissues and fat are liquefying; purge fluid (dark reddish-brown or blackish liquid from lungs/stomach) has frothed or leaked from mouth, nose, and any orifices, mixing with bathtub water into a thick, greasy, chunky soup. Hair may still be attached but scalp and facial skin are detaching. Soft tissues feel soft and gaseous or mushy when disturbed. If any insects gained access earlier, fly larvae (maggots) would be active in orifices and wounds, feeding and further accelerating soft-tissue loss; otherwise the process is purely bacterial and algorithmic.

Depending on water level, “washerwoman” maceration of hands and feet makes the epidermis white, swollen, wrinkled, and easily stripped. Bones and teeth remain, but connective tissues and ligaments are weakening. There is often a strong ammonia-like or fecal undercurrent as nitrogenous compounds break down, layered under the dominant rot.

**The smell is overwhelming, penetrating, and physically nauseating**—a thick miasma that hits before visual confirmation. It is a complex, dense mixture of putrescine and cadaverine (the classic “rotting flesh” amines), hydrogen sulfide (rotten eggs), mercaptans, skatole, indole, short-chain fatty acids, and sulfurous volatiles. The overall character is sweet-cloying at the edges yet sharply putrid and glass-cutting in intensity: like the worst combination of spoiled meat left in sun, sewage, and decomposing vegetables, but denser and more animal. It coats the tongue and sinuses, sticks to clothes and hair, and can trigger gagging or vomiting on instinct. Even after leaving the room the odor clings and returns in waves. In a confined bathroom it saturates everything—steam, towels, grout—and can be noticeable in adjacent spaces or hallways long before the door is opened.

For narrative use: the character would probably catch the thick, acidic-sweet sewer-meat reek first through the door or under it, feel it coat the back of the throat, then open the door to the full visual of the blackened, ballooned form half floating or slumped in cloudy black fluid, skin sliding, grimace distorted by gas, with the stench rising in a physical wave that forces a step back or retch. Temperature, humidity, clothing, bacterial load, and whether the tub drains or retains water can accelerate or modulate slight details, but a week is reliably advanced into these stages indoors.

**The dim basement reeked of mildew and cigarette smoke. Rain hammered the street grating above, distant and useless.**

Ricca stood over Harmon, who was duct-taped to a scuffed wooden chair, wrists raw, a black eye already swelling shut. The debt collector—mid-thirties, scar across one knuckle, expression flat as wet concrete—rolled his shoulders and tapped the Louisville Slugger against his palm. The wood made a dull, solid *thok* each time.

“Last chance,” Ricca said, voice low. “The eight grand. Plus the vig. You had until midnight.”

Harmon spat blood. “I—I’m good for it tomorrow. My guy comes through—”

Ricca didn’t wait. He stepped in, planted his feet, and swung the bat like he was clearing brush. It connected with Harmon’s right knee—a thick, wet *CRACK* that echoed off the cinderblock walls, sharp as a branch snapping under ice. Bone shattered under aluminum-jacketed ash. Harmon’s scream tore out raw and high, decking the air; his body jackknifed against the tape, thigh muscle jumping like a dying fish. The chair legs scraped. Cartilage ground. A secondary wet *pop* followed as the joint folded wrong.

“Fuck—please—*ahhChrist*—” Harmon’s voice cracked into a gurgle. Tears mixed with snot. His free leg kicked uselessly. The sound of the break kept ringing in his ears, wet and wrong.

Ricca didn’t pause for drama. He reset his grip, exhaled, and brought the bat down again—this time higher, across the left shin. *THWACK-CRUNCH*. The tibia gave with a deeper, splintering noise, like green wood fracturing. Harmon’s scream this time was wordless, animal, pure agony. He convulsed so hard the chair tipped; only duct tape kept him upright. Legs hanging at unnatural angles, white bone not quite piercing skin but swelling black already under blood-slick pants. He retched, bile and blood spattering the concrete. Breath came in frantic hitches—fast, shallow, drowning.

Ricca wiped that first fleck of blood off the bat with a rag, calm as washing dishes. “Payment on Tuesday or I finish the set. Next time I aim higher.”

Harmon wet himself. The only sounds left were his broken sobbing, the rain, and the slow drip of the leaky pipe. The bat rested against the wall. Ready.
